doc.title: Alan Broadbent interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 26, 2023

chapter: New Zealand and the road to jazz
title: The deep swing feeling: Armstrong, Bud Powell and Tristano
summary: Broadbent explains the 'deep swing' he seeks, tracing it from Louis Armstrong through Lester Young, Bird and Bud Powell, and mentions studying with Lennie Tristano.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I want to pursue that for a moment. The feeling, ‘cause I think I know what you mean, is it about swing?

It’s a deep swing. It’s a very deep relationship. I’ll give you the people, well the man that invented it was Louis Armstrong of course. You can hear that in his — well there’s YouTube of him doing “Dinah” with his group somewhere in Copenhagen or something. And his — you know his group is chugging along [scats] but Louis, when he starts to impro— even with a few notes — where he puts those notes are, they’re like, I don’t know, a tension-release thing you know when his more complicated phrases happen they still have that feeling of bouncing around the ring, bouncing back into the center. And those — the lineage of that, not just my opinion — there’s Lester Young and of course Bird and Bud Powell. Bud for me and for a lot of like-minded people, Bud is the one where it was no longer ornamental music. It was no longer Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, magnificent pianists that they are. This was a speaking voice, like a horn. And Bud introduced that by way of, all right if you want Earl Hines and Nat Cole, Bud even sits at the piano kind of like Nat Cole. But it was Bud and the relationship to the deep, deep time that you can hear when he’s not sick, when he’s in great form. Those are the things that are precious to me and separated from all other music. So that’s what I mean. You know of course I listen to all kinds of music and love it. You know I can love charts by David Rose or Percy Faith, you know it’s the orchestration and the music, whatever. But when it comes to what Tristano called a life force, this life force that he believed was a human need, I don’t know, in us. Art. The movement of music, deep music you know. I’m not talking about dance music or Beyoncé or whatever. Fine, whatever. I’m talking about dancing in the mind and in the heart. And — well Bud Powell said he wished it was treated with the seriousness of purpose with which he meant it.
Well said. Nice quote. The person that you mentioned — we had a slight cutoff in the connection — and you said this quote from someone.
I studied with him for a few years.
